summary: Outpost Academy is a free 3D game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a small base on the Moon, alone or with friends. You play a cadet at Shackleton crater, near the south pole, and Captain Nova gives you missions: build solar panels, oxygen makers and soil shields, scan things to learn real science, and get to the shelter with your crew when a solar storm hits. Every storm starts from a real solar flare, from NASA’s DONKI database or NOAA’s satellites when NASA is down. Power, air and shielding are always pulling against each other, so kids have to plan and make trade-offs, like a real crew would. Finishing tasks earns stars, a Moon medal and science cards. It runs in the browser on school laptops and tablets, with nothing to install and no account.
details:
Outpost Academy is a 3D browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 learn real space science by completing real missions on the moon.

F.A. picked this challenge because he loves Minecraft and has already built a game that teaches kids electronics. He was the lead game designer and tester, and Abdullah, his mentor, helped him build it. We used an AI agent to explore game styles and mechanics, prototyped a few options, then picked one and committed to it. The first version was rough, it wasn’t clear what to do and the graphics were poor. So we kept playing and fixing, testing with two younger players and feeding their feedback into each update, and added better graphics, a multiplayer mode and a map.

How it plays. Captain Nova leads the Moon mission and tells every player what each mission needs. You walk the base, clean and build solar panels, build oxygen makers and soil shields, and balance three resources: power, air and a shield against radiation. A short prologue and six missions each teach one idea, from keeping the power on through the lunar night to dropping a supply crate with no parachute, because there’s no air on the Moon. Before each big decision the game shows the maths, so kids work it out themselves. Tasks earn stars toward a Moon medal, scanning uncovers 12 science cards with real facts, and the medal screen sums up what the player learned.

What’s new. Designed by a kid for kids, he decided what to put in and what not to add, what is important and what is not. The learning is built into the missions, kids pick up real science by completing tasks, not by reading lessons. And the game focuses on collaboration and team work for survival in space rather than competition!

Real data. The game asks NASA’s DONKI database for the biggest solar flare of the last 30 days. A bigger flare means a stronger storm, so you need a thicker shield or a faster run to the shelter. If NASA doesn’t answer it uses NOAA’s satellite data, and offline it uses a saved real flare, always saying which on screen.

What we considered. We followed the challenge’s rules: ages 7 to 12, three resources to manage, and every choice has a cost. It’s safe for children (team play has no chat and no player names), accessible (subtitles always on, playable with sound off, a calm view, and gentle failure, where Nova explains and you retry), and honest about what’s live, saved or simplified.

Impact. We want kids to feel what a real crew feels: resources in space are limited, there’s never enough power, air or time, and good planning keeps people safe. And because the challenges and data in the game are real, kids get a real sense of what life is like for astronauts out there!

Tools. JavaScript, HTML, CSS and three.js, hosted on Vercel with small server routes for NASA data and team play, plus Upstash Redis to share a base. Sound uses the Web Audio API and spoken lines use the Web Speech API. It works on laptops and tablets, with game controller support. AI agents helped with coding, 3D models, pictures and voices.

For judges: JUDGE QUICK START on the title screen jumps into any mission. Next, we’d like to add a Mars base and a teacher view for whole classes.

NASA Curiosity RAD: radiation on the Mars surface
